stem: A 20-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of wheezing and shortness of breath that are worse at night and in the early morning. Each episode resolves spontaneously without treatment, and he remains completely asymptomatic between attacks. Physical examination between episodes is normal. There is no history of acute airway swelling, skin rash, or hypotension during episodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
stemHtml: A 20-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of wheezing and shortness of breath that are worse at night and in the early morning. Each episode resolves spontaneously without treatment, and he remains completely asymptomatic between attacks. Physical examination between episodes is normal. There is no history of acute airway swelling, skin rash, or hypotension during episodes. What is the most likely diagnosis? (Question Id: 505038)
keywords: Recurrent wheezing + dyspnea → suggests episodic obstructive airway disease
Night + early morning worsening → classic circadian bronchial asthma pattern
Asymptomatic between attacks → reversible airway obstruction
Normal exam between episodes → intermittent disease (not structural lung disease)
keywordsHtml:
1. Recurrent wheezing + dyspnea → suggests episodic obstructive airway disease
  2. Night + early morning worsening → classic circadian bronchial asthma pattern
  3. Asymptomatic between attacks → reversible airway obstruction
  4. Normal exam between episodes → intermittent disease (not structural lung disease)

E.title: Bronchial asthma
E.body: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder characterized by hyperresponsiveness of bronchial smooth muscle leading to episodic, reversible airflow obstruction. Patients typically present with wheeze, dyspnea, and chest tightness that vary over time. Symptoms classically worsen at night and early morning due to circadian variation in bronchial tone and reduced endogenous corticosteroids. Between episodes, patients are completely asymptomatic and examination is often normal.
E.bodyHtml: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder characterized by hyperresponsiveness of bronchial smooth muscle leading to episodic, reversible airflow obstruction. Patients typically present with wheeze, dyspnea, and chest tightness that vary over time. Symptoms classically worsen at night and early morning due to circadian variation in bronchial tone and reduced endogenous corticosteroids. Between episodes, patients are completely asymptomatic and examination is often normal.
E.clinicalReasoning: This is the classic diagnostic pattern of bronchial asthma. The combination of nocturnal worsening, episodic wheeze, and complete symptom-free intervals strongly confirms reversible airway hyperreactivity. No alternative option explains all features together.
E.clinicalReasoningHtml: This is the classic diagnostic pattern of bronchial asthma. The combination of nocturnal worsening, episodic wheeze, and complete symptom-free intervals strongly confirms reversible airway hyperreactivity. No alternative option explains all features together.

A.title: Vocal cord dysfunction
A.body: Vocal cord dysfunction involves paradoxical adduction of vocal cords during inspiration leading to episodic dyspnea and upper airway obstruction symptoms. It often presents with inspiratory stridor rather than expiratory wheeze. It is commonly triggered by stress or exercise and resolves rapidly once the episode ends.
A.bodyHtml: Vocal cord dysfunction involves paradoxical adduction of vocal cords during inspiration leading to episodic dyspnea and upper airway obstruction symptoms. It often presents with inspiratory stridor rather than expiratory wheeze. It is commonly triggered by stress or exercise and resolves rapidly once the episode ends.
A.clinicalReasoning: Although episodic, it produces upper airway symptoms (stridor, throat tightness) rather than true wheeze. No nocturnal pattern or classic bronchial reversibility is described.
A.clinicalReasoningHtml: Although episodic, it produces upper airway symptoms (stridor, throat tightness) rather than true wheeze. No nocturnal pattern or classic bronchial reversibility is described.

B.title: Anxiety-related dyspnea
B.body: Anxiety-related dyspnea is a functional breathing disorder associated with panic or stress episodes. Patients experience subjective breathlessness, hyperventilation, palpitations, and fear of dying. Physical examination and lung auscultation remain normal.
B.bodyHtml: Anxiety-related dyspnea is a functional breathing disorder associated with panic or stress episodes. Patients experience subjective breathlessness, hyperventilation, palpitations, and fear of dying. Physical examination and lung auscultation remain normal.
B.clinicalReasoning: This does not produce true wheezing or objective airflow obstruction. The presence of recurrent wheeze strongly argues against this diagnosis.
B.clinicalReasoningHtml: This does not produce true wheezing or objective airflow obstruction. The presence of recurrent wheeze strongly argues against this diagnosis.

C.title: Gastroesophageal reflux–induced bronchospasm
C.body: GERD can trigger bronchospasm via vagal reflexes or microaspiration, particularly at night when supine. Patients may have chronic cough, nocturnal symptoms, and sometimes wheeze. Associated symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, or sour taste.
C.bodyHtml: GERD can trigger bronchospasm via vagal reflexes or microaspiration, particularly at night when supine. Patients may have chronic cough, nocturnal symptoms, and sometimes wheeze. Associated symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, or sour taste.
C.clinicalReasoning: This is a plausible mimic of asthma but lacks consistent classic episodic reversible wheeze pattern and no reflux symptoms are mentioned.
C.clinicalReasoningHtml: This is a plausible mimic of asthma but lacks consistent classic episodic reversible wheeze pattern and no reflux symptoms are mentioned.

D.title: Hyperventilation syndrome
D.body: Hyperventilation syndrome is characterized by episodic dyspnea due to excessive ventilation leading to respiratory alkalosis. Symptoms include dizziness, chest tightness, tingling, and anxiety. It is not associated with true airway obstruction.
D.bodyHtml: Hyperventilation syndrome is characterized by episodic dyspnea due to excessive ventilation leading to respiratory alkalosis. Symptoms include dizziness, chest tightness, tingling, and anxiety. It is not associated with true airway obstruction.
D.clinicalReasoning: This does not cause wheezing or nocturnal bronchospasm. Therefore, it is inconsistent with the stem findings.
D.clinicalReasoningHtml: This does not cause wheezing or nocturnal bronchospasm. Therefore, it is inconsistent with the stem findings.

keyConcept: Bronchial asthma is diagnosed clinically by recurrent episodes of wheezing and dyspnea that worsen at night/early morning and completely resolve between attacks due to reversible airway hyperreactivity.

diagram.name: Bronchial Asthma – Clinical Diagnosis (Episodic Nocturnal Wheeze Pattern)
diagram.caption: This diagram illustrates the classic clinical presentation and diagnostic pathway of bronchial asthma as an episodic, reversible airway disease. It highlights key features such as recurrent wheezing, shortness of breath, nocturnal and early morning worsening, and complete symptom-free intervals between attacks.
